title: Latent heat

2026-11-01T08:14:09Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: Neither bank point teaches latent heat: the calorimetry point covers heat from temperature change (q = mcΔT) and the enthalpy point covers reaction heat, so no bank point teaches energy absorbed or released at constant temperature during a change of state (Q = mL).

draft.title: Latent heat
card: During a change of state, such as ice melting or water boiling, energy goes in or out but the temperature stays constant. The energy changes how the particles are arranged, not how fast they move.
the energy absorbed or released when a substance changes state at constant temperature. Melting and boiling absorb it. Freezing and condensing release it.
Q = mL, where Q is the energy in joules, m is the mass in kilograms and L is the specific latent heat in joules per kilogram.
L depends on the substance and the change. For water, melting ice takes about 3.3 × 10^5 J/kg. Boiling takes about 2.3 × 10^6 J/kg, which is much more.
draft.remember: During a change of state the energy goes into changing particle arrangement, so temperature stays constant. Use Q = mL.

a.q: A block of ice at 0 °C is heated and begins to melt. What happens to the energy supplied while it melts?
opts: It changes the particle arrangement, not the temperature
It raises the temperature of the ice until it is all melted
It is lost to the surroundings and does not affect the ice
It makes the particles move faster, so the water gets hotter
a.why: During melting, the energy goes into changing how the particles are arranged, so the temperature stays at 0 °C. The tempting option says the temperature rises, but the temperature is constant during a change of state.
a.clue: Look at what stays constant during a change of state.

b.q: Priya heats 0.50 kg of water at 100 °C until it has all boiled to steam at 100 °C. About how much energy is needed, using L = 2.3 × 10^6 J/kg?
b.why: Q = mL = 0.50 × 2.3 × 10^6 = 1.15 × 10^6 J, which is about 1.2 × 10^6 J. Using 2.3 × 10^6 J ignores the mass and gives the energy for 1 kg.
b.clue: Multiply the mass by L, and check the mass is not 1 kg.

a.best: It changes the particle arrangement, not the temperature
